newsitem.title: USA: Reno says affirmative action still needed.
newsitem.headline: Reno says affirmative action still needed.

text.p: Attorney General Janet Reno said Wednesday that affirmative action programmes continue to be needed to help minorities and women overcome discrimination that still exists in the country.

Outlining her civil rights views in a speech at a Baptist church in Birmingham, Alabama, Reno denounced as "misguided" proposals by the Republican-controlled Congress to curtail or end altogether affirmative action by the federal government.
She acknowleged that critics believe affirmative action is unfair, giving special preferences to minorities or women while holding non-minorities accountable for events that happened long ago.

"However, the fact that many minorities and women are still struggling at the bottom of the economic ladder suggests that this criticism misses the mark -- society's reality belies all the purported special treatment for minorities," she said.
A prepared text of the speech, Reno's first major address devoted solely to civil rights, was released by the Justice Department.
Reno said concerns about affirmative action often reflected "misperceptions" and added that any abuses could be fixed.
"When affirmative action is done right, there are no quotas, there are no preferences for the unqualified and the programmes end when their objectives have been achieved," she said.
Her remarks closely followed President Clinton's declared policy in July of 1995 to "mend, not end" affirmative action.

Reno said much progress has been made in civil rights over the past 40 years, but added that prejudice, intolerance and discrimination still exist and that more needs to be done over the next four years.

"We cannot say that we have completed our journey when even today blacks and Hispanics -- and in many cases, women -- still have a harder time getting into college, renting an apartment, getting a job or obtaining a loan," she said.

Reno vowed to work especially hard on fair housing and fair lending, affirmative action in employment and other areas, equal educational opportunities and building trust between the police and minorities.
"The next four years will see our continued attack on the legacy of discrimination that has created so much inequality and that continues to have a devastating impact on our society," she said.
